Regard
rē-gärd´
v.t. (to look upon, to esteem, to have respect unto; rendering Hebrew ra'ah, shur, Greek epiblepō, ameleō)
From the French regarder, to look at. In Scripture regarding is never neutral looking; it is looking with esteem, and God's regard falls where men do not expect it.

Biblical Definition

To regard is to look upon a thing with esteem, and Scripture uses it to describe where God's eye rests and what a man's eye is fixed on. Mary's song reports God's direction of gaze: “he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luk 1:48) — He looked at the least likely house in Israel. The psalmist reports the fatal direction of a man's own gaze: “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Psa 66:18) — not the presence of sin, which is in every heart, but sin regarded, cherished, held on to and looked at with favour. Wisdom records being ignored: “I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” (Pro 1:24). And Hebrews quotes God's reciprocal withdrawal from a covenant-breaking generation: “because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord” (Heb 8:9). Whom God regards and what a man regards are the two questions the word puts, and the second decides whether prayer is heard.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines regard as to look towards, to observe, to esteem, to have respect to, and to pay attention to as a matter of importance.

expand to see more

REGARD, v.t. To look towards; to point or be directed.

2. To observe; to notice with some particularity.

3. To attend to with respect and estimation; to value.

4. To attend to as a thing that affects our interest.

5. To keep; to observe with religious or solemn attention.

Key Scripture

Luk 1:48 — "For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed."

Psa 66:18 — "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:"

Pro 1:24 — "Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;"

Heb 8:9 — "Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 66:18 is heard as a threat that any remaining sin blocks prayer, which drives sincere believers to despair; the verse is about sin regarded — cherished and looked at with favour — not sin present and fought.

expand to see more

The misreading is common and it wounds tender consciences. If the verse meant that a man with any sin in his heart cannot be heard, no prayer would ever ascend, since indwelling sin remains in the holiest believer until glory. The Hebrew is about looking at iniquity with approval — keeping it in view, guarding it, refusing to part with it. A Christian who hates his sin, confesses it, and fights it is not the man described; the man described is the one who has made peace with a sin and prays anyway. The difference is the whole difference between David in Psalm 51 and Saul at Endor.

Luke 1:48 supplies the encouraging half of the doctrine. God regards the low estate — the unimportant house, the unnoticed servant, the congregation nobody writes about. This is a settled pattern rather than an exception: He resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble, and He chose the weak things of the world to confound the mighty. Where a man's eye rests determines whether he is heard; where God's eye rests is settled by grace, and it has never yet rested where the world expected.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, look upon, regard; Greek epiblepō (G1914), to look upon with favour, and ameleō (G272), to be careless of — the direction of the eye, divine and human.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, look at, regard; “if I regard iniquity in my heart” (Psa 66:18).

Greek epiblepō (G1914) — to look upon, regard with favour; “he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden” (Luk 1:48).

Greek ameleō (G272) — to neglect, be unconcerned; “I regarded them not” (Heb 8:9).

Usage

"“He hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden” — where God's eye rests."

"“If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” — sin cherished, not sin present."

"“I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” — wisdom ignored."
